title: Constraints on type parameters (class, struct, new(), notnull)
hook: Without a where clause, T is barely more useful than object. Constraints tell the compiler what operations T supports — construct it, compare it, treat it as an enum, or even allow a ref struct.

blocks.text: A constraint is a rule on a type parameter, written after where T : .... It unlocks members on T inside the generic body. where T : class means T is a reference type. where T : struct means a non-nullable value type. where T : new() requires a public parameterless constructor. where T : notnull rejects nullable types (as a warning). where T : unmanaged means a blittable value type. You can also constrain to a base class, interface, Enum, Delegate, or another type parameter U.

entries.plainDefinition: Syntax that restricts what types can replace a type parameter T.
entries.example: where T : IComparable<T> lets you call a.CompareTo(b).

entries.plainDefinition: A constraint meaning T cannot be a nullable reference or nullable value type. Violations produce a warning, not an error.
entries.example: where T : notnull is how Dictionary keys stay honest with nullable reference types.

entries.plainDefinition: An anti-constraint that opts in to ref struct type parameters like Span<T>. Must come last and cannot combine with class.
entries.example: void Slice<T>(T value) where T : allows ref struct accepts ReadOnlySpan<char>.

blocks.text: Unconstrained T can only do what object can do — ToString, GetHashCode, Equals. Constraints are how you write Max<T> that compares values, Create<T>() that constructs instances, or Hash<T> that requires notnull. Interviews expect you to name the catalog, know the exclusion rules (struct cannot pair with new()), and understand that notnull warns instead of errors. The allows ref struct clause exists so generic parsers can accept Span-like types without breaking ref safety.

blocks.title: Constraint ordering rules
blocks.body: At most one of struct, class, class?, notnull, unmanaged — and that one comes first. new() must be last among ordinary constraints. allows ref struct comes after everything. struct and unmanaged already imply a constructor story and cannot combine with new().

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Need to call a method on T?
items.body: Constrain to an interface: where T : IComparable<T> unlocks CompareTo.

items.title: Need to construct T?
items.body: Add where T : new() — but not with struct or unmanaged, and not for types with required members.

items.title: Need a value type only?
items.body: Use where T : struct for any non-nullable value type, or unmanaged for blittable types.

items.title: Need nullable safety?
items.body: where T : notnull warns if someone passes string? or int?. Pair with nullable attributes on return types.

diagram.title: Constraint categories
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  T[Type parameter T] --> K[Kind constraints]
  T --> B[Base constraints]
  T --> S[Special constraints]
  K --> K1[class / struct / notnull / unmanaged]
  B --> B1[Base class / interface / Enum / Delegate]
  S --> S1[new / allows ref struct / naked U]

snippet.label: Constraints you actually write
snippet.explanation: IComparable unlocks CompareTo. new() unlocks new T(). Enum and Delegate are real base constraints. notnull is a nullable-reference-types safety net.

snippet.label: Exclusions that fail to compile
snippet.explanation: struct and unmanaged already guarantee a parameterless constructor, so new() is redundant and illegal. Types with required members cannot satisfy new() because the compiler cannot guarantee a valid instance.

snippet.label: Equality trap on class-constrained T
snippet.explanation: == on a class-constrained T uses reference identity, even when T is string with an overloaded ==. Use IEquatable<T> when you mean value equality.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Using == on a class-constrained T and expecting string-style value equality. Writing where T : struct, new() — struct already implies a parameterless constructor. Expecting new() to work with types that have required properties. Using T? on an unconstrained T as a cache-miss signal — prefer TryGet or a Result wrapper.

interviewTakeaways: Constraints unlock operations on T; unbounded T is object-like.
struct / unmanaged / new() have exclusion rules; new() last; allows ref struct last of all.
notnull warns; required members block new(); Enum and Delegate constraints are first-class.
commonPitfalls: Using == on a class-constrained T and expecting String overload behavior.
Expecting new() to work with required properties.

jsTsCorrelations.note: function f<T extends Foo>(x: T) is the TypeScript analogue of where T : Foo. TypeScript has no struct, unmanaged, or ref struct story.
